newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia's 1996 trade gap tops $2.26 billion.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia's 1996 trade gap tops $2.26 billion.

text.p: Yugoslavia's trade deficit last year reached $2.26 billion and some analysts said it would continue to grow in 1997.
According to data published by the federal statistical office, 1996 exports were worth $1.84 billion, while imports $4.1 billion.
Export growth rate was stagnating and well below the targeted 50 percent rise, while imports rose more rapidly, exceeding the projected $3.5 billion for 1996.
"If last year's trend continues, the deficit could expand," Zivojin Jevtic of the Institute for Foreign Trade told Reuters.
Imports surged by nearly $5O million in December to $396 million compared to the previous month's $348 million, while exports dropped to $168 million from $179 million.

To reduce the deficit Yugoslavia needs to restore economic ties with former trading partners, other ex-Yugoslav republics and membership in international financial institutions and the World Trade Organisation (WTO), Jevtic said.
The Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce late last year said exports could rise by as much as 48 percent in 1997 since raw materials and semi-manufactured goods accounted for the bulk of last year's imports.
Other economists said the trade gap could start narrowing as sources for financing it are depleted.

"Without capital and foreign investment it will be difficult to sustain a deficit of this size, and any growth will require the same or even higher exports," said Pavle Petrovic of the independent economics institute Ces Mecon.

The trade gap has mostly been financed from unofficial hard currency reserves held abroad by Yugoslav banks and companies after a war-related international trade embargo was imposed on the new federation, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, in 1992.
The embargo was lifted in 1996 but major commercial and trade ties have not been restored to date.
"The deficit will be one of the basic problems of economic development in 1997, and the government's economic policy does not outline how it will be resolved or eased," Petrovic said.

Economists agreed sizeable growth depended on radical reform including liberalisation of trade and privatisation which Serbia, the bigger of the two republics, has been slow to undertake as state managers are reluctant to relinquish their grip on the economy.
To achieve the 48 percent official targeted export growth, around $2.7 billion would have to be exported this year, Jevtic said.

"This requires imports of as much as $6 billion, which would mean a deficit of more than $3 billion. The real question is from where will such high imports be financed since they are growing faster than exports."
Official forecasts see GDP growth at around 13 percent in 1997, with industrial output rising 10.8 percent.
"If GDP is now around 50 percent below the level before the break-up of former Yugoslavia in 1991, how can production be increased to ensure such high exports?" Jevtic said.
Serbia accounted for around a third, or $20 billion, of ex-Yugoslavia's GDP before its break-up in 1991, and for around $4 billion of its $11 billion exports.
"To return to this level would mean doubling production, but lack of capital and investment will remain major barriers for this," Jevtic said.
-- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
